original_quotes.quote: C.2.2 Backend Integration We retain failure-driven SkillBank expansion and skill retrieval for SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . For ExpeL ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , we retain trajectory-based reflection, successful-experience retrieval, and insight-bank updates. The integrated interface names its operations Agree , Remove , Edit , and Add . For Shared Reflexion, we retain Reflexion’s failure-to-corrective-plan feedback mechanism ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . The remaining changes are backend-specific. Our SkillRL integration excludes the supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning stages of the complete training pipeline. ExpeL’s experience gathering and insight extraction are interleaved with online task acquisition rather than executed as separate stages. Shared Reflexion extends task-local episodic memory to a cross-task retrievable memory. Consequently, the experiments evaluate SPG-Select with the skill-evolution mechanisms of SkillRL, ExpeL, and Shared Reflexion, rather than exact reproductions of their complete original pipelines.

Practice and evaluation. During practice, the task-selection policy selects a task and the agent makes one attempt using its current backend state. For each backend-benchmark comparison, every policy first receives the same N N warmup interactions. The backend state produced by this common warmup initializes the ensuing T T -round policy comparison. SPG-Select uses the observed outcome to compute the surrogate-progress feedback defined in Section 3 , namely the temporal difference between consecutive profile estimates. This feedback is computed from the outcome before the trajectory is used for the subsequent backend update. Actor-model parameters remain fixed, so adaptation takes place through accumulated skills, insights, or reflections. After practice, we freeze the resulting backend state and evaluate each held-out task with a single attempt. No updates or test-time reflection retries are performed during evaluation. This protocol measures the transfer of acquired knowledge to held-out tasks. Metrics. We report the terminal task success rate as a percentage of the evaluation pool. ALFWorld success is determined by the environment’s task-completion signal. WebShop success requires a terminal reward of 1.0 1.0 , and partial rewards do not count as successes. For WebShop, we also report Score, the mean terminal reward expressed as a percentage, which preserves partial credit. We additionally report ALFWorld results by task family to examine variation across task types. All reported gains are percentage-point differences computed from unrounded rates. Random seeds. The main results in Table 1 are reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across three random seeds. All other experimental figures and tables in the main text and appendix use a single fixed random seed shared across the compared methods. Skill-evolution backends. Prompt B.1: Failure Reflection and New-Skill Generation Analyze these failed agent trajectories and suggest NEW skills to add to the skill bank. FAILED TRAJECTORIES: {failure_examples} EXISTING SKILL TITLES (avoid duplicating these): {existing_titles} Generate 1– {max_new_skills_per_update} NEW actionable skills that would help avoid these failures. Each skill must have: skill_id , title (3–5 words), principle (1–2 sentences), and when_to_apply . Use skill IDs: {available_dynamic_skill_ids} . Return ONLY a JSON array of skills, with no other text. Example format: [{"skill_id": "dyn_001", "title": "Verify Object Location First", "principle": "Before attempting to pick up an object, verify its current location by examining the environment.", "when_to_apply": "When a task requires moving an object but its location is uncertain"}] Newly generated skill example. The following skill was generated for this appendix using the schema in Prompt B.1. It is an illustrative output, separate from the skills used in the reported experimental runs. At runtime, the updater replaces the illustrative identifier with the next unused dyn_NNN identifier. Field Newly generated value skill_id dyn_001 title Require Observable State Change principle After an action intended to alter the world, compare the next observation with the pre-action state and treat the transition as unconfirmed unless a goal-relevant change is visible. If no change is observed, repair an unmet precondition or choose another admissible action instead of advancing the plan. when_to_apply After an open, take, place, heat, cool, clean, or variant-selection action whose success is required by a later step.

C.4.1 Successful Held-Out Evaluation Cases The cases below show every interaction step in each successful trajectory, with model thoughts omitted. Observations are abbreviated from the persisted evaluation logs for presentation. Ellipses shorten long room inventories, option lists, or product lists without omitting any interaction step. Each member s ∈ 𝒮 evo s\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{evo}} evolves during training through two complementary channels: its LoRA adapter ϕ s \phi_{s} is distilled from the investigator’s own calls, and its skill card, a short list of Report and Ignore rules appended to the role instruction q s q_{s} , is revised by a reflector model (Sec. 4.2 ). Visual artifacts are the cues that shift most rapidly as generators improve, and the calls issued by the investigator expose exactly the inputs, scopes, and difficulty levels on which the inspectors are consulted. The audio tools and the PaddleOCR detector remain fixed: their outputs are measurements, such as speaker attributes, transcripts, and text boxes, whose meaning should not drift while the investigator learns to interpret them, and the scarcity of labeled audio forgeries would make their adaptation unreliable. The investigator itself is optimized with reinforcement learning, so the system improves both in what it asks and in what it is told.
